 On Your Side: Medicare enrollment deadline approaches; how to compare your options 
 By Frances Watson Published : Nov. 13, 2026 at 5:06 PM CST | Updated : 11 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - Choosing Medicare coverage can be confusing, even for people enrolled for years. As the annual open enrollment deadline approaches, a Medicare agent recommends researching plans and asking questions before choosing.
 Barbara Bowling has relied on Medicare for nearly a decade, but she said she still worries about whether she has the right coverage and what she might pay for medications and specialist visits.
 “What if a chronic illness happens and my plan doesn’t come up to par? So I guess the part that scares me the most is the decision-making,” Bowling said.
 Medicare agent Roy Rickstrew said understanding how a plan works is important because choosing coverage without knowing the details can be costly.
 “There’s Advantage and Supplement plans. Both of them work fine if you understand them,” Rickstrew said. “But unfortunately, if you get into one of these and you don’t understand how it operates, it can be a costly mistake.”
 Rickstrew said people should review provider networks and prescription costs when comparing their options. He said Medicare.gov is a place to start, but cautioned that its provider listings may not always be accurate.
 He also recommends calling your doctor’s office directly to confirm it accepts the plan you’re considering and to ask whether any changes are expected.
 “If you’re not going to talk to an agent, call your doctor, confirm that they do, in fact, take the plan,” Rickstrew said.
 Medicare’s annual open enrollment period runs from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. During that time, people can make certain changes to their Medicare health and drug coverage. Different enrollment rules apply in other circumstances.
 For Bowling, the most important step is taking the time to compare options.
 “Do your research. Just sit down with a cup of coffee, turn the TV off, and do your research,” she said.
